flawed_step: The step needed for any proof — that the degree sequence determines which vertices are adjacent in a tree (up to isomorphism) — cannot be justified. The degree multiset records only how many vertices have each degree, not how they are connected.
counterexample: Tree A on {1..6}: edges 1-2, 1-3, 1-4, 4-5, 5-6. Degrees: deg1=3, deg4=2, deg5=2, deg2=deg3=deg6=1, so the sequence is (3,2,2,1,1,1). Tree B on {1..6}: edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 1-5, 5-6. Degrees: deg1=3, deg3=2, deg5=2, deg2=deg4=deg6=1, so the sequence is (3,2,2,1,1,1). Both are connected with 6 vertices and 5 edges, so both are trees. An isomorphism preserves degrees and adjacency, so it would have to map the two degree-2 vertices of A onto the two degree-2 vertices of B while keeping their adjacency. In A, vertices 4 and 5 are adjacent; in B, vertices 3 and 5 are not. So A and B are not isomorphic. (A is a centre with branches of lengths 3,1,1; B has branches of lengths 2,2,1.)
assessment_summary: False. Two 6-vertex trees both have degree sequence (3,2,2,1,1,1) but are not isomorphic: their degree-2 vertices are adjacent in one tree and not in the other.
